lessons.culture: Asked "شلونك؟", Iraqis nearly always answer "الحمد لله" or "زين" whatever they feel, and add "وإنت؟" back. Close friends and family then ask "شبيك؟" if something looks wrong, and saying "زعلان" or "تعبان" plainly is normal only with people you trust.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "شلونك اليوم؟". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; "زين، الحمد لله" is what Iraqis actually say.

exercises.tip: "الحمد لله" follows almost every "I'm fine".

exercises.prompt: A friend asks: "شبيك؟" You are just a little tired. Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Formal and stiff; "ولا شي" and "شوية" are the spoken words.

exercises.tip: A woman says "تعبانة".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "آني ___ مرة، أريد آكل شي." Meaning: I'm very hungry, I want to eat something.

too_formal.feedback: Formal way to state hunger; "جوعان" is the everyday word.

exercises.tip: "جوعان" for a man, "جوعانة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "آني ___ من الامتحان." Meaning: I'm worried about the exam.

too_formal.feedback: Nobody speaks like this out loud; it belongs in writing.

exercises.tip: ق is said as g in Baghdad: "galgaan".

too_formal.feedback: "سعيد" is the formal word; Iraqis say "مبسوط".

exercises.tip: "مرة" and "هواية" both mean very, a lot.

exercises.tip: "آني" first, then the feeling, then how much, then when.

lessons.culture: Iraqis say "عندك حق" very often, even in the middle of an argument, and soften a "no" with "يمكن، بس" or "مو هيچ". Among friends a plain "لا" is fine, but with elders or strangers people add "بس" and a smile.

exercises.tip: "عندچ حق" to a woman.

too_formal.feedback: Formal and stiff; "مو هيچ" is the everyday way.

exercises.tip: "مو" is the Iraqi "not" before a word.

lessons.culture: Iraqis give advice freely, from family to neighbours to the taxi driver, and it usually comes with "إن شاء الله" at the end. "دير بالك" means both "take care of yourself" and "watch out", and it is also a common way to say goodbye.

exercises.prompt: A friend says: "آني تعبان هواية". Give advice.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; Iraqis say "لازم".

exercises.tip: "لازم" plus the verb gives "you should".

exercises.prompt: A friend says: "عندي وجع راس". Suggest a medicine.

exercises.tip: "جرب" is the masculine command, "جربي" the feminine.

exercises.tip: "على كيفك" means at your own pace.

too_formal.feedback: Formal; the spoken phrase is "دير بالك".

lessons.culture: In Iraq you call a waiter or shopkeeper "أستاذ" and open a complaint with "لو سمحت", and the answer is usually "ولا يهمك" or "تفضل". Complaints stay gentle, since raising your voice at someone serving you is seen as rude.

challenge.title: How Was Your Week?
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation between two friends who run into each other. One asks how the other is feeling, hears about a problem, gives some advice, and the other politely raises one more small complaint before agreeing on what to do.
required_elements: a question asking how someone feels, using "شلونك" or "شلونچ"
at least one feeling word such as "تعبان", "مبسوط" or "قلقان"
a piece of advice using "لازم" or "أحسن شي"
agreement or disagreement using "عندك حق" or "مو هيچ"
a polite complaint opened with "لو سمحت" or "آسف على الإزعاج"
